terms.gloss: the private parts (here a girl’s or woman’s)
evidence: Varr. RR 2.4.10: nātūram quā fēminae sunt
terms.comment: The decent word of Cicero and Varro, for either sex. It names the whole, which is what a parent usually means by “vagina”.

terms.gloss: a woman’s or girl’s private parts
terms.comment: Tacitus’s word; the counterpart of virīlia.

terms.gloss: a little girl’s private parts, in nurses’ talk
terms.comment: Varro reports that women, nurses above all, call a little girl’s parts “piglet”, as Greek women say choeros. Otherwise porcus is simply a pig.
Classically a scabbard, and so the anatomists’ word; its one bodily use in Plautus is an obscene joke.
Lewis & Short: “as an obscene word, avoided acc. to Cic.”. Latin says nōbīscum, not cum nōbīs, Cicero explains, because the sounds would run together obscaenius (Or. 154).
Not the English vulva: in Latin the womb, and a sow’s womb as a delicacy (Hor. Ep. 1.15.41, Mart. 13.56.2).

phrases.latin: nostrae mulierēs, maximē nūtrīcēs, nātūram quā fēminae sunt in virginibus appellant porcum
phrases.english: our women, and nurses above all, call the part that makes little girls female porcus
